summary.text: The divisibility assumption implies that no odd prime divisor \(p\) of \(n\) can divide \(a(n-1)\); but if \(n=pc\) is composite with \(p\) odd, Fermat’s theorem makes the factors indexed by multiples of \(p-1\) supply one more factor of \(p\) than occurs in \((n-1)!\), while the remaining case \(n=2^e\) is excluded by \(v_2(a(2^e-1))=e-1\), obtained from the binary digit-sum formula for factorial valuations. Once \(n=p\) is prime, any proper order \(d<p-1\) of \(2\) modulo \(p\) would put the factor \(2^d-1\) in the numerator of \(a(p-1)\), and since \(p\nmid(p-1)!\) this would force \(p\mid a(p-1)\), contradicting the same exclusion; hence the order is \(p-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 A_N=2^{N-1}\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(N\geq 1).
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
 a(N)=\frac{A_N}{N!}.
\]
We first establish that this quotient is an integer and collect the divisibility facts about it that will be needed.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). We will use the standard factorial valuation formula
\[
 v_p(m!)=\sum_{j\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^j}\right\rfloor.
\]
Equivalently, if \(s_p(m)\) denotes the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(m\), then
\[
 (p-1)v_p(m!)=m-s_p(m).
\]
In particular, for \(m\geq1\), the digit sum is at least \(1\), so
\[
 (p-1)v_p(m!)\leq m-1,
\]
and hence
\[
 v_p(m!)\leq \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{1}
\]
(The corresponding assertion for \(m=0\) is immediate.) We will also use the recurrence obtained directly from the factorial valuation formula:
\[
 v_p(m!)=\left\lfloor\frac m p\right\rfloor+v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac m p\right\rfloor!\right). \tag{2}
\]

We next prove a basic lower bound for the valuation of the product in \(A_N\). If \(p\) is an odd prime, Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 p\mid 2^{p-1}-1.
\]
Since \(x-1\mid x^j-1\) for every \(j\geq1\), it follows that
\[
 p\mid 2^{j(p-1)}-1 \qquad(j\geq1). \tag{3}
\]
Put
\[
 M=\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
For each \(j=1,\ldots,M\), the integer \(j(p-1)\) belongs to the interval \(1,\ldots,N-1\), and these indices are distinct. Therefore (3) supplies at least one factor of \(p\) from each of \(M\) distinct factors in the product. Consequently,
\[
 p^M\mid\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1). \tag{4}
\]

This proves the integrality of \(a(N)\). Indeed, for an odd prime \(p\), (1) and (4) show that the product supplies at least \(v_p(N!)\) factors of \(p\). For \(p=2\), the factor \(2^{N-1}\) supplies at least \(v_2(N!)\) factors of \(2\), because (1) gives \(v_2(N!)\leq N-1\). Thus, prime by prime,
\[
 N!\mid 2^{N-1}\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1)=A_N.
\]
In particular, for every \(N\geq1\), \(a(N)\) is a positive integer and satisfies the exact identity
\[
 a(N)N!=2^{N-1}\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1). \tag{5}
\]

A useful immediate consequence of (5) is the following. If \(p\) is prime and
\[
 p^{v_p(N!)+1}\mid\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1), \tag{6}
\]
then \(p\mid a(N)\). In fact, (6) and (5) imply
\[
 v_p(a(N))+v_p(N!)=v_p(A_N)\geq v_p(N!)+1,
\]
so \(v_p(a(N))\geq1\).

We now derive the main divisibility statement used to exclude composites:

**Lemma 1.** If \(p\) is an odd prime and \(c\geq2\), then
\[
 p\mid a(pc-1). \tag{7}
\]

Set \(N=pc-1\). By (2), since
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{pc-1}{p}\right\rfloor=c-1,
\]
we have
\[
 v_p(N!)=v_p((c-1)!)+(c-1). \tag{8}
\]
Also,
\[
 N-1=pc-2=c(p-1)+(c-2),
\]
so
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 =c+\left\lfloor\frac{c-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{9}
\]
Applying (1) to \((c-1)!\) gives
\[
 v_p((c-1)!)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{c-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{10}
\]
Combining (8)--(10),
\[
 v_p(N!)+1
 \leq c+\left\lfloor\frac{c-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
By (4), the product \(\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1)\) is therefore divisible by \(p^{v_p(N!)+1}\). The consequence (6) proves (7).

We also need a version for a prime argument itself.

**Lemma 2.** Let \(p\) be prime. If
\[
 1\leq k<p-1\quad\text{and}\quad p\mid 2^k-1,
\]
then
\[
 p\mid a(p-1). \tag{11}
\]

Indeed, none of \(1,2,\ldots,p-1\) is divisible by \(p\), so
\[
 v_p((p-1)!)=0.
\]
The factor \(2^k-1\) occurs in
\(
\prod_{j=1}^{p-2}(2^j-1)
\), because \(1\leq k<p-1\). Thus this product is divisible by \(p=p^{v_p((p-1)!)+1}\), and (6), with \(N=p-1\), gives (11).

The remaining auxiliary fact handles powers of two.

**Lemma 3.** For every \(e\geq2\),
\[
 2^e\nmid a(2^e-1). \tag{12}
\]

Put \(N=2^e-1\). Every number \(2^k-1\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2\left(\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}(2^k-1)\right)=0. \tag{13}
\]
The binary expansion of \(N=2^e-1\) consists of exactly \(e\) digits, all equal to \(1\). Hence its binary digit sum is \(s_2(N)=e\). The factorial digit-sum formula therefore gives
\[
 v_2(N!)=N-s_2(N)=N-e. \tag{14}
\]
Taking \(2\)-adic valuations in (5), and using (13) and (14), gives
\[
 v_2(a(N))+(N-e)=N-1.
\]
Thus
\[
 v_2(a(2^e-1))=e-1,
\]
which proves (12).

We now prove the conjecture. Let \(n>2\), and assume
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{15}
\]
First observe that if \(p\) is an odd prime divisor of \(n\), then
\[
 p\nmid a(n-1). \tag{16}
\]
For otherwise, (15) would imply
\[
 p\mid 2^{n-2}.
\]
A prime dividing a power divides its base, so this would give \(p\mid2\), contrary to \(p\) being odd.

We claim that \(n\) is prime. Suppose to the contrary that it is composite. There are two cases.

First suppose that \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(p\). Since \(n\) is composite and \(p\) is prime, \(p<n\). Write
\[
 n=pc.
\]
Then \(c\geq2\). Lemma 1 gives
\[
 p\mid a(pc-1)=a(n-1),
\]
contradicting (16).

It remains to consider the case in which \(n\) has no odd prime divisor. By unique factorization, all prime factors of \(n\) are then equal to \(2\), so
\[
 n=2^e
\]
for some integer \(e\geq0\). Since \(n>2\), necessarily \(e\geq2\). For such \(e\),
\[
 e\leq 2^e-2=n-2. \tag{17}
\]
This inequality is immediate at \(e=2\), and thereafter follows by induction, since doubling \(2^e\) increases the right-hand side much faster than increasing \(e\) by one. It follows from (17) that
\[
 2^e\mid2^{n-2}. \tag{18}
\]
On the other hand, substituting \(n=2^e\) into (15) gives
\[
 2^e\mid a(2^e-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Together with (18), this implies
\[
 2^e\mid a(2^e-1),
\]
contradicting Lemma 3. Both composite cases are impossible, and therefore \(n\) is prime.

It remains to show that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\). Since \(n>2\) is prime, \(2\not\equiv0\pmod n\), and its multiplicative order modulo \(n\) is defined. Let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2).
\]
By Fermat's little theorem,
\[
 2^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so \(d\mid n-1\). In particular, \(d\leq n-1\). Suppose that \(d\neq n-1\). Then
\[
 1\leq d<n-1
\]
and, by the defining property of the multiplicative order,
\[
 n\mid2^d-1.
\]
Lemma 2, applied with \(p=n\) and \(k=d\), now yields
\[
 n\mid a(n-1). \tag{19}
\]
But \(n\) is an odd prime divisor of itself, so (16), with \(p=n\), says precisely that \(n\nmid a(n-1)\). This contradicts (19). Hence
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_n(2)=n-1.
\]
Finally, because \(n\) is prime, \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Thus the order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) is \(\varphi(n)\), which is exactly the assertion that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Therefore, for every integer \(n>2\), if
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2},
\]
then \(n\) is prime and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), as claimed.
